newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Analysts say Bulgaria 1997 budget bill unrealistic.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say Bulgaria 1997 budget bill unrealistic.

text.p: Bulgaria's 1997 draft budget approved by the cabinet on Friday is based on unrealistic assumptions, analysts said on Saturday.
"The assumptions in this budget bill were valid in November, but now are outdated," Krassen Stanchev, director of the Institute for Market Economics, an independent think-tank, told Reuters.
"The draft has the nature of a theoretic exercise with unrealistic figures," said Stanchev.
The budget bill assumes a lev/dollar rate of 500, the implementation of a currency board and a deficit of 6.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). GDP is estimated at 4.585 trillion levs.
The lev was quoted at a new all-time low of around 650 to the dollar on Saturday from 70 a year ago.
Year-on-year inflation in December in the budget frame is seen at 72 percent. Year-on-year inflation in 1996 is expected at around 300 percent. It was 257 percent in November.
Bulgaria has agreed to introduce a currency board system proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to boost confidence in the slumping lev and the crumbling financial system.
But economists say there are many flaws in the hurried preparation of Bulgaria's currency board plan and chances of its success with this budget are very slim.
Analysts say the plan's intoduction, initially planned for February, will be most likely delayed by political instability.
A new Socialist cabinet is expected to be formed by mid-month after Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned two weeks ago due to what he said was lack of support of his policies.
"Even if the Socialist-dominated parliament passes this 1997 budget bill, it will not be obligatory for the next government. It will have to be revised," said Stanchev.

Expenditure is assumed at 1.225 trillion levs and revenue at 909 billion levs. Most of the revenue is expected to come from privatisation proceeds, but the government has not yet approved this year's privatisation programme.

Pari financial daily said tax revenue was seen at 26 percent of GDP. Foreign debt payments are estimated at 4.5 percent of GDP, and interest payments on domestic debt are estimated at 484.75 billion levs.
The budget also envisages unprecedented cuts of public service employees of about 60,000 by March.
The government, said that beside the draft 1997 budget, it will introduce to parliament in the next few days a package of legal amendments to make the currency board operational.
Cash-strapped Bulgaria relies entirely on external funding for pending foreign debt payments of $300 million due in the first quarter of this year.
However, quick implementation of a currency board accompanied by delayed structural reforms is a major precondition of the multilateral lenders.
